rationale: B wins because it knows where the facts stop. A's "Mindbody Owns the Studio Software, the Consumer Marketplace, and Now the AI That Fills Both" is the shiny overreach: ownership of ClassPass is real, but interaction with the AI is not established. B's refusal - "The only supplied fact is that Mindbody owns ClassPass; how the assistant interacts with ClassPass inventory was not supplied" - is the adult move, and its kept angles stay closer to what a reporter can verify.
gaps_in_A: "Mindbody Says AI Cut Fitness No-Shows by 22% - and It's Rolling Out to 50,000 Studios" overclaims distribution. The update says Mindbody powers booking for over 50,000 studios and salons; it does not say this assistant is rolling out to all of them.
"Mindbody Owns the Studio Software, the Consumer Marketplace, and Now the AI That Fills Both" turns ClassPass ownership into an implied product relationship. Clever sentence, weak footing.
"While Fitness Apps Race to Build AI Coaches" imports a broader consumer-AI race that was not supplied. It can work only with a real comparison or current coverage, not vibe.
"Bundled pricing / AI monetization angle" was refused as too thin, but bundled pricing is a real SaaS-business angle if paired with competitor add-on proof.
gaps_in_B: "What happened when a studio let an AI text its waitlist" is useful only after a named studio exists. B admits "Without a named studio this angle does not exist" but still counts it as a kept angle.
"The software behind 50,000 studios" sands off the source fact. Mindbody powers over 50,000 studios and salons; the wording makes the footprint narrower and cleaner than the update allows.
"The prevailing pattern that reporter is tracking is AI as a paid add-on or premium tier" is plausible, not supplied. The angle needs examples before it leaves the building.
"a private owner doesn't have to show public markets an AI revenue line" is a smart inference near the edge of fact. It needs ownership and take-private context before a reporter sees it.
